Law of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem

STAT 2103

Law of Large Numbers

Suppose the overall distribution of systolic blood pressure for adults in the US is approximately Normal(mean=120, sd=10).

For any individual person, systolic blood pressure might be near 120, or above or below.

We can randomly sample one person and measure their systolic blood pressure:

set.seed(6292)
x<-rnorm(n=1, mean=120, sd=10)
print(x)
## [1] 125.4235

Instead, we could go out and measure the blood pressure of 5 randomly selected people, and record the average:

set.seed(6292) #setting the "seed" makes the random number generator 
            # give you the same values
            # every time you run this chunk of code

x<- rnorm(n=5, mean=120, sd=10) #this simulates sampling 5 people

print(x)
## [1] 125.4235 122.4917 120.5572 138.3784 124.4839
print(mean(x)) #this is the average of the sample
## [1] 126.2669

The average for those randomly selected 5 people is roughly 126.

What if we randomly select another 5 people and take the average of their blood pressure measurements?

x<- rnorm(n=5, mean=120, sd=10) #this simulates sampling 5 people

print(x)
## [1] 124.34793 137.02585 133.96347 121.07864  99.12466
print(mean(x)) #this is the average of the sample
## [1] 123.1081

For this new random sample of 5 people, the average blood pressure was slightly different.

Now, what if we keep doing this many times? Collect many different random samples of 5 people, and record the averages. What values of the sample average do we tend to get?

n_repetitions<- 200 # let's repeat the 5-person-sample exercise 200 times

sample_means<-rep(0,n_repetitions) #create a vector to store our 200 sample means

for(i in 1:n_repetitions){
  sample_means[i] <- mean(rnorm(n=5, mean=120, sd=10))
}

The ``for loop” in this chunk does the following: for each of the 200 repetitions we want to perform, draw a sample of 5 people’s blood pressure, then record the average, and store it in the “sample_means” vector. At the end, we have 200 sample means, each of which is the average blood pressure of a sample of 5 randomly-selected people.

We can visualize the results with a histogram:

hist(sample_means, xlab="Average BP of 5 people", xlim=c(105, 135))

What if, instead of taking 5 person samples, we take 20 person samples? That is, we randomly select 20 people, measure their blood pressure, and record the average.

We can simulate one repetition of this process:

x <- rnorm(n=20, mean=120, sd=10)
print(x) #this prints all 20 of the blood pressure values
##  [1] 138.7624 126.2880 136.9819 125.8467 132.9821 103.1890 116.0709 122.3216
##  [9] 124.4871 144.8772 121.2014 136.2679 119.1894 150.3449 103.0968 129.5688
## [17] 113.7506 125.0998 109.5187 133.3536
print(mean(x)) #this prints the sample average for the 20-person-sample
## [1] 125.6599

We can repeat the above, drawing a new sample of 20 people:

x <- rnorm(n=20, mean=120, sd=10)
print(mean(x)) #this prints the sample average for the 20-person-sample
## [1] 121.247

Then, like above, we can imagine repeating this process, taking many different samples of 20 people, and recording the sample average for each sample:

n_repetitions<- 200 # repeat the 20-person-sample exercise 200 times

sample_means<-rep(0,n_repetitions) #create a vector to store our 200 sample means

for(i in 1:n_repetitions){
  sample_means[i] <- mean(rnorm(n=20, mean=120, sd=10))
}

… and visualize the results with a histogram:

hist(x=sample_means, xlab="Average BP of 20 people", xlim=c(105, 135))

Compared to the example with 5-person-samples, 20-person-samples tend to produce sample averages that are clustered more closely around 120, which is the average of the overall population.

Taking this even further, what would it look like with 1000 person samples?

n_repetitions<- 200 # repeat the 20-person-sample exercise 200 times

sample_means<-rep(0,n_repetitions) #create a vector to store our 200 sample means

for(i in 1:n_repetitions){
  sample_means[i] <- mean(rnorm(n=1000, mean=120, sd=10))
}

hist(sample_means, xlab="Average BP of 1000 people", xlim=c(105, 135))

The sample average blood pressure of 1000 people tends to be very close to the population average. For a sample of 1000 people, it’s rare for the sample average to be less than 118 or more than 122.

(back to board)

Distribution of the Sample Average

Because blood pressure is normally distributed with mean 120 and standard deviation 10, the average blood pressure of a random sample of 5 people is also normally distributed, with mean 120 and standard deviation 10/sqrt(5).

We can generate a large number of 5-person-samples and take their averages, like we did above, and compare it to the normal distribution with mean 120 and standard deviation 10/sqrt(5)

n_repetitions<- 2000 # let's repeat the 5-person-sample exercise 2000 times

sample_means<-rep(0,n_repetitions) #create a vector to store our 2000 sample means

for(i in 1:n_repetitions){
  sample_means[i] <- mean(rnorm(n=5, mean=120, sd=10))
}
hist(sample_means, probability=TRUE, xlab="Average BP of 5 people") 
#this is a histogram of our 2000 observed sample averages

curve(dnorm(x, mean=120, sd=10/sqrt(5)), add=TRUE) 

#this is the curve of the normal distribution probability density function

Central Limit Theorem

Next let’s consider a variable whose population distribution is NOT normal: income. In the US, the population distribution of adults’ income is skewed, with a long right tail (a small number of people with very large incomes).

Suppose the expected value is 70, and the standard deviation is 37.4 (thousands of dollars).

curve(dgamma(x, shape=70*0.05, rate=0.05), from=1, to=200, 
      main="Population Distribution of Income", 
      xlab= "Income (in 1000 USD)", ylab="p(x)")

If we randomly sample people and record their income, the distribution of the individual incomes will be skewed, no matter how much data we collect.

hist(x= rgamma(n=50, shape=70*0.05, rate=0.05), 
     main="50 Randomly Sampled Incomes", xlab="Income (1000 USD)")

hist(x= rgamma(n=200, shape=70*0.05, rate=0.05), 
     main="200 Randomly Sampled Incomes", xlab="Income (1000 USD)")

hist(x= rgamma(n=1000, shape=70*0.05, rate=0.05), 
     main="1000 Randomly Sampled Incomes", xlab="Income (1000 USD)")

The central limit theorem does NOT say that the individual samples become normally distributed when we collect enough data.

But the sample AVERAGE starts to look normally distributed, for large enough samples.

Suppose we randomly sample 3 adults and record their average income. What types of values do we get for that sample average?

n_repetitions<- 1000 # let's repeat the 3-person-sample exercise 1000 times

sample_means<-rep(0,n_repetitions) #create a vector to store our 1000 sample means

for(i in 1:n_repetitions){
  sample_means[i] <- mean(rgamma(n=3, shape=70*0.05, rate=0.05))
}
hist(x= sample_means, main="", xlab="Average Income of 3 people (1000 USD)", 
     probability = TRUE)

The average income of a sample of 3 people still looks a bit skewed (longer right tail). This doesn’t look like a normal distribution.

What about the sample average of 10 people?

n_repetitions<- 1000 # let's repeat the 10-person-sample exercise 1000 times

sample_means<-rep(0,n_repetitions) #create a vector to store our 1000 sample means

for(i in 1:n_repetitions){
  sample_means[i] <- mean(rgamma(n=10, shape=70*0.05, rate=0.05))
}
hist(x= sample_means, main="", xlab="Average Income of 10 people (1000 USD)", 
     probability=TRUE, breaks=15)

What about the sample average of 50 people?

n_repetitions<- 1000 # let's repeat the 50-person-sample exercise 400 times

sample_means<-rep(0,n_repetitions) #create a vector to store our 400 sample means

for(i in 1:n_repetitions){
  sample_means[i] <- mean(rgamma(n=50, shape=70*0.05, rate=0.05))
}
hist(x= sample_means, main="", 
     xlab="Average Income of 50 people (1000 USD)", 
     probability=TRUE,breaks=15)
curve(dnorm(x, mean=70, sd=sqrt(20*70/50)), add=TRUE)
legend("topright", legend=c("Normal(70, 37.4/sqrt(50))"), bty='n', lty=1)

Even though the population distribution of incomes is not normal, and is noticeably skewed, the average income of 50 random people is starting to look like a normal distribution.

The curve superimposed on the histogram is the normal distribution pdf with expected value 70 and standard deviation 37.4/sqrt(50).
